cards.title: Fire prevention and life safety
cards.summary: Every building must meet the UP Fire and Emergency Services Act 2022 and Rules 2024; the owner or occupier is liable, and the completion certificate depends on compliance.
conditions: The completion certificate is not issued until the Authority is satisfied that fire safety is complied with (§10.1.2, p.121).

Minimum standards depend on building height, covered area and occupancy; the list includes access, exits, smoke management, extinguishers, hose reels, detection and alarm, sprinklers, hydrants, water storage, fire lifts, standby power and refuge area (§10.2.1, p.122).

Existing buildings are treated by class: those approved without a fire NOC are assessed against the standards in force when approved; structural changes are not mandatory for access and exit (§10.3.1, p.123).
The height and area thresholds that trigger each item are in the UP Fire Rules 2024, which are not loaded here. No figures are shown.

cards.title: Heritage sites and riverbanks
cards.summary: No permission inside the prohibited area of an ASI-protected monument; the regulated area needs an Archaeology Department no-objection.
conditions: Prohibited area of protected monuments: no development or building permission. Regulated area: permission on the basis of a no-objection from the Archaeology Department under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act 1958 (§2.10, p.38).
Other important buildings and sites: the Authority may set conditions for conservation of cultural, historical and architectural heritage (§2.10(ii), p.38).

Ganga: within 200 m of the bank, only repair, renovation and conservation of existing buildings; pilgrimage-site monasteries, ashrams and temples allowed at coverage 35% and FAR 1.5 with an approved no-pollution plan and no direct drainage into the river (§2.11, pp.38–39).
Other rivers: follow any NGT or court order received by the Authority (§2.11(iii), p.39).
Building height near monuments, airport funnel zones and other statutory limits is governed by distance from them (§4.3.7, p.85).

cards.title: Permissions, appeals and architectural control
cards.summary: Standard designs get automatic approval on small residential plots; completion certificate decisions can be appealed.
conditions: Residential buildings on plots up to 300 sq m built to the Authority's standard designs need no separate building map approval (§2.7.2.1, p.32).
No separate permission to use a residence as a creche, home-stay or paying guest accommodation if parking is adequate; professionals may use up to 25% of FAR (p.32).
A rejected completion certificate can be re-applied for after the reasons are resolved, and appealed to the Chairman within 30 days of the rejection order (§2.9.3.7–2.9.3.8, p.38).
Partial completion certificate: only when infrastructure for the part is developed and functional, and proportional EWS and LIG buildings are complete (§2.9.3.9, p.38).
Architectural control: the Authority may notify facade, height, cornice and colour rules for an identified area; deviation is a violation of the Act (§2.12, p.39).

cards.title: Meerut Master Plan 2031 (draft): FAR for surrendered open space
cards.summary: An owner who hands over park or open-space land receives extra floor area to use outside the built-up area.
conditions: Extra FAR equals the residential maximum, scaled by the ratio of circle rates; total FAR is capped at 1.25 times normal (§15.9.6, p.144).

flags.title: TOD FAR is stated two ways
flags.detail: NCRTC's document quotes the UP TOD Policy as allowing FAR of up to 5 in the TOD zone. The Byelaws 2025 instead give TOD FAR as 150% to 350% of base FAR by road width, and unrestricted on 45 m roads: group housing in a non-built-up area on a 24 to 45 m road has a base of 2.50 and a maximum of 8.75.
flags.standing: The Byelaws say State sectoral policies prevail where the two differ (clause 1.6, p.19). The TOD Policy 2022 itself is not loaded, so check its current text before relying on either figure.

flags.title: The Meerut plan gives two widths for the track strip
flags.detail: Page 118 says the influence zone covers 50 m on either side of the track; page 135 says 500 m. Both give 1.5 km at stations and a total of 4,890 ha.
flags.standing: An inconsistency inside one draft document. The map uses 500 m.

flags.title: Corridor width differs between the Meerut plan and the Regional Plan
flags.detail: The Meerut plan draws its influence zone 500 m either side of the RRTS track. The Draft Regional Plan 2041 encourages intense development up to 1 km on either side of rail transit corridors.
flags.standing: The Regional Plan prevails within NCR (rule R1), but the 2041 plan is a draft and does not bind yet.

flags.title: Meerut's mixed-use roads are tighter than the Byelaws 2025
flags.detail: The Meerut plan caps commercial and group housing complexes on its mixed-use roads at 40% coverage and FAR 2.0, with parking of 2 car units per 100 sq m. The Byelaws 2025 allow coverage up to the setback lines and a maximum FAR for mixed use of 2.00 to 8.75 by road width, unrestricted on 45 m roads.
flags.standing: No rule in the loaded documents says which prevails between the Byelaws and a master plan. Both are shown; this needs the Authority's reading.

flags.title: This location is in a TOD influence zone: higher FAR is unlocked
flags.detail: Inside a TOD zone the Byelaws 2025 raise the maximum FAR to 150%, 250% or 350% of base by road width, unrestricted on 45 m roads, at the ordinary purchasable-FAR charge.
flags.standing: Applies once the zone is included in the master plan or notified (§8.2.1, p.113). The Meerut and Ghaziabad plans that show these zones are drafts.

flags.title: An older FAR notification may be superseded
flags.detail: The Byelaws 2025 prevail over the earlier orders and byelaws listed in their Appendix-1 (clause 1.5, p.19). Check whether the notification on FAR in group housing maps is on that list.
